label: Person
name: Abdullah ibn Salam
summary:
Abdullah ibn Salam (c. 595–663 CE) was a prominent Jewish rabbi of Medina who converted to Islam and became one of the most respected companions of the Prophet Muhammad. Born Al-Husayn ibn Salam into a Jewish family of the Qaynuqa tribe in Medina, he was a scholar of the Torah and had been awaiting, according to later tradition, the arrival of the final prophet based on scriptural signs he had identified.

His conversion is regarded as significant in Islamic tradition both for his standing as a Jewish scholar whose acceptance of Muhammad's prophethood validated the claim that Islam fulfilled earlier scripture, and for his own character — Muhammad reportedly declared that he was among those guaranteed paradise. He participated in Islamic scholarship and is credited with transmitting hadiths that are included in all six canonical Sunni collections.

Abdullah ibn Salam occupies a significant position in the history of Jewish-Muslim relations and in the Islamic theology of scriptural fulfilment. His story — a learned Jew recognising Muhammad's prophethood in the Torah — became a foundational narrative in Islamic apologetics and in the tradition of interfaith conversion narratives. He is honoured in both Sunni and Shia traditions, and his reported certainty about Muhammad's truth has been cited across Islamic history as testimony to Islam's validity.
